flashcards.back: WEF is a built-in Windows feature in which source computers push chosen events to a central Windows Event Collector (WEC) server through subscriptions. For Sentinel you can install the Azure Monitor Agent on the WEC server and use a data collection rule to send the forwarded events, rather than installing the agent on every source machine, which suits large fleets and servers where an agent is not allowed.
flashcards.detail: Contrast with the Windows Security Events via AMA connector, where the agent runs on each machine and a DCR picks the event sets or XPath filters to collect.

flashcards.front: Collecting Azure activity and resource logs with Azure Policy
flashcards.back: The Azure Activity connector streams subscription-level control-plane events into the AzureActivity table. Azure resource connectors stream resource diagnostic logs by using Azure Policy to apply one log-streaming (diagnostic setting) configuration to all current and future resources of a type within a scope, which needs the Owner role on the policy assignment scope. Resource diagnostic logs usually land in AzureDiagnostics or resource-specific tables.
flashcards.detail: Without Policy you would create a diagnostic setting by hand on every resource; Policy also remediates new resources automatically. These connectors do not support DCR transformations.

flashcards.front: KQL jobs in the Sentinel data lake
flashcards.back: KQL jobs run one-time or scheduled asynchronous queries on data lake tables and federated tables (such as Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft 365, and Resource Graph data) and are suited to long investigations, historical threat intelligence matching, and joins or unions across many tables. A job can promote results to the analytics tier as a new table (named with a _KQL_CL suffix) or append to an existing one, so you can then hunt and alert on it.
flashcards.detail: Promote only the columns and rows you need because analytics-tier storage costs more than the lake. Use KQL jobs for up to 12 years of data, summary rules for frequent summarization (for example every 20 minutes), and search jobs for archived data or hydrating one big table.

flashcards.front: Summary rule tables (updated detail)
flashcards.back: Summary rules aggregate high-volume data on a schedule into custom summary tables in the analytics tier, so dashboards, hunting, and detections query a small table. They can read from Analytics, Auxiliary, Basic, and data lake tables (but not System tables), run as often as every 20 minutes, and have out-of-the-box templates.
flashcards.detail: They suit workspaces not onboarded to the data lake, such as when the source is on a Basic or Auxiliary plan.

flashcards.front: Security Copilot agents in the Defender portal
flashcards.back: Security Copilot agents automate SOC tasks and are deployed from Security Copilot > Security Store in the Defender portal, then set up from Security Copilot > Agents. In Defender they include the Phishing Triage Agent (extended as the Security Alert Triage Agent), the Threat Intelligence Briefing Agent, the Security Analyst Agent, the Dynamic Threat Detection Agent, and the Threat Hunting Assistant. Agents consume Security Compute Units (SCUs) and authenticate with a dedicated Microsoft Entra Agent ID agent identity or a connected user account.
flashcards.detail: Eligible Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 customers receive Security Copilot with 400 SCUs per month for every 1,000 paid user licenses, up to 10,000 SCUs per month, at no additional cost.

flashcards.front: Sentinel MCP server
flashcards.back: Microsoft Sentinel's Model Context Protocol (MCP) support is a hosted, Entra-authenticated server offering scenario-focused tool collections, so AI clients and agents can query Sentinel data lake and Defender data in natural language without knowing table schemas or writing KQL. Compatible hosts include Visual Studio Code, Security Copilot, Copilot Studio, and other MCP-capable AI clients.
flashcards.detail: In MCP terms the AI application is the host, it runs an MCP client per connection, and the Sentinel server provides the tools. It needs no infrastructure deployment from you.

flashcards.front: Case management in the Defender portal
flashcards.back: Case management manages SecOps work natively in the Defender portal. Incident cases (preview, and the recommended experience for incidents) are created from correlated incident activity and track ownership, severity, status, classification, tasks, comments, activity history, custom fields, and resolution. Generic cases are created manually for other SecOps work. Case templates configure custom fields and SLA policies.
flashcards.detail: Incident case access uses the unified RBAC permissions Security Data Read (view) and Security Data Manage (view and manage), the same model as the legacy incident experience, which remains available during preview.

flashcards.front: Device timeline in Defender for Endpoint
flashcards.back: The Timeline tab of a device page shows a chronological view of the events and associated alerts observed on that device, so an analyst can follow a suspected attack step by step. You can filter by event type, review the MITRE ATT&CK techniques linked to events, open process trees, and flag events for follow-up.
flashcards.detail: The timeline can show activity that is newer than the device page's Last seen value, so trust the timeline when the two disagree.

flashcards.front: Purview Insider Risk Management and DLP alerts in Defender XDR
flashcards.back: Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management alerts appear in the Defender portal under Incidents & alerts, can be grouped with DLP and Microsoft Entra ID alerts in one incident, can be filtered by service source, and stay synchronized with Purview. Analysts can hunt for all activity tied to the user in the alert. DLP alerts are handled the same way, with remediation in place on users, files, and devices.
flashcards.detail: A built-in alert tuning rule for DLP signals takes effect in early October 2026: it sets them as behaviors, so they stop generating alerts and incidents but remain in BehaviorInfo and BehaviorEntities. Disable the rule under Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Alert tuning to keep DLP alerts.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Purview Audit (Standard vs. Premium)
flashcards.back: Purview Audit records user and admin activity in the unified audit log and is enabled by default. Audit (Standard) retains records for 180 days and supports the audit search tool, the Audit Search Graph API, and the Search-UnifiedAuditLog cmdlet. Audit (Premium) includes all of that, keeps records up to one year (ten years with an add-on), and offers audit log retention policies and higher bandwidth access to the Office 365 Management Activity API.
flashcards.detail: For a business email compromise investigation, audit records of mailbox rule changes and sign-ins from the unified audit log often provide the timeline; if the event is older than the retention window it is gone.

flashcards.front: Content search in Purview eDiscovery
flashcards.back: Microsoft Purview eDiscovery lets investigators search Exchange Online mailboxes, SharePoint sites, OneDrive, Teams, Microsoft 365 Groups, and Viva Engage in one search and export results. Classic Content Search, classic eDiscovery (Standard), and classic eDiscovery (Premium) were retired on August 31, 2025 (except for Microsoft 365 operated by 21Vianet); content search features now live in the search experience of the new eDiscovery, including a Content Search case.
flashcards.detail: Access requires membership in the eDiscovery Manager role group in the Purview portal. Content search finds items in place; it does not itself investigate sign-in or API activity, which come from audit and Graph logs.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Graph activity logs
flashcards.back: Microsoft Graph activity logs are an audit trail of every HTTP request the Graph service processes for a tenant, from apps, SDKs, scripts, and Microsoft portals. They are off until a tenant admin enables them with a diagnostic setting that sends them to Log Analytics, storage, or Event Hubs; this needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 and Security Administrator is the least privileged supported role. In Log Analytics they appear in the MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs table with fields such as AppId, UserId, ServicePrincipalId, IPAddress, RequestUri, and ResponseStatusCode.
flashcards.detail: They show what a stolen token or malicious app actually did through the API, such as mass mailbox reads, which sign-in logs alone do not reveal. Advanced hunting has a related GraphAPIAuditEvents table.

flashcards.front: Investigating incidents with agentic AI
flashcards.back: Embedded Security Copilot and its agents speed up investigations: the Security Analyst Agent runs ready-made or custom analyses (anomaly detection, clustering, risk scoring) on Defender, Sentinel Log Analytics, or data lake data from a prompt or from Analyze with copilot in advanced hunting; the Threat Hunting Assistant turns natural language into KQL and interprets results; the Dynamic Threat Detection Agent raises alerts for gaps it finds with MITRE-mapped explanations. Incident cases can also run agentic playbooks and show agent session output.
flashcards.detail: An analyst remains responsible for validating what an agent concludes before acting. Agents consume SCUs and run under an agent identity or a connected user account.

flashcards.front: Releasing actions taken by automatic attack disruption
flashcards.back: Containment taken by automatic attack disruption, such as a contained user account or an isolated device, appears in the incident and in the Action center. An analyst reviews the incident evidence, and if the detection is judged a false positive, undoes the action from the Action center so the user or device regains access.
flashcards.detail: Excluding a device or user from disruption in the configuration is a preventive control; releasing the action in the Action center is the corrective one after the fact.

flashcards.front: Hunting graph in Defender XDR
flashcards.back: The hunting graph renders threat scenarios in advanced hunting as an interactive graph of entities and relationships, so an analyst can trace paths and possible choke points and take actions on results that tabular KQL output might hide. Open it from Investigation & response > Hunting > Advanced hunting using the hunting graph icon. It depends on the Microsoft Sentinel data lake and at least read-only access to Microsoft Security Exposure Management.
flashcards.detail: Use it to see how entities connect (for example a user with privileged access paths to a critical asset), instead of joining many tables by hand.

flashcards.front: Blast radius analysis in the incident graph
flashcards.back: Blast radius analysis extends the incident graph in Defender to show the vulnerable paths an attacker could take from a compromised entity to a critical asset, so one consolidated graph shows the current impact of a breach and the possible future impact. It is powered by Microsoft Sentinel graph and is auto-provisioned when you already have the Sentinel data lake.
flashcards.detail: Blast radius is about what could happen next; the hunting graph is the analyst-driven exploration tool. Purview Insider Risk Management has a similar data risk graph for data leak blast radius.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Sentinel graph and custom graphs
flashcards.back: Microsoft Sentinel graph models assets, identities, activities, and threat intelligence as nodes and edges, answering questions such as what the blast radius of a compromised account or document is. Custom graphs (preview) are authored in a Jupyter notebook with the Microsoft Sentinel extension for Visual Studio Code, published and materialized by a graph job, and queried with Graph Query Language (GQL) on the Graphs page in the Defender portal.
flashcards.detail: On-demand graph jobs keep a graph for 30 days, while scheduled graph jobs rebuild it on your refresh schedule. Usage is billed under the Sentinel graph meter.

flashcards.front: EntraIdSignInEvents (replaces AADSignInEventsBeta)
flashcards.back: EntraIdSignInEvents is the advanced hunting table for Microsoft Entra interactive and non-interactive sign-ins, and EntraIdSpnSignInEvents covers service principal and managed identity sign-ins. The AADSignInEventsBeta table is deprecated on October 19, 2026, when queries that use it are migrated automatically to EntraIdSignInEvents.
flashcards.detail: In a Sentinel workspace the equivalent tables are SigninLogs and the non-interactive and service principal sign-in log tables; the Entra-prefixed tables are the Defender XDR advanced hunting names.

flashcards.front: Choosing the right advanced hunting table
flashcards.back: Match the question to the table: UrlClickEvents for Safe Links clicks from email, Teams, and Office apps; EmailEvents, EmailAttachmentInfo, and EmailUrlInfo for messages, attachments, and URLs; DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents, and DeviceLogonEvents for endpoint activity; IdentityLogonEvents and IdentityQueryEvents for Active Directory authentication and directory queries; CloudAppEvents for cloud app activity; GraphAPIAuditEvents for Microsoft Graph API requests; AlertInfo and AlertEvidence for alerts.
flashcards.detail: When a case needs both a click and its landing activity, join UrlClickEvents to DeviceNetworkEvents or EmailUrlInfo on the URL or user instead of searching one table broadly.

flashcards.front: Hunting with notebooks on the data lake and the Sentinel MCP server
flashcards.back: Notebooks over the Sentinel data lake are Jupyter notebooks run through the Microsoft Sentinel extension for Visual Studio Code using PySpark on Spark compute, suited to low-and-slow attack detection, anomaly and machine learning analysis, and visualization across large data. An MCP client such as VS Code can additionally connect to the Sentinel MCP server so an AI assistant can query the same lake data in natural language.
flashcards.detail: Notebook jobs can be scheduled, and you can promote findings to the analytics tier with a KQL job for alerting.

flashcards.front: KQL jobs vs. summary rules vs. search jobs (when to hunt with which)
flashcards.back: Use a KQL job for up to 12 years of lake data with full KQL, joins, and unions, one-time or scheduled. Use a summary rule for frequent aggregation (as often as every 20 minutes) of Analytics, Basic, Auxiliary, or lake data into analytics-tier summary tables. Use a search job for data in the archive tier (or older than your data lake onboarding date) and to hydrate a large volume from a single table into a new table.
flashcards.detail: If the question mentions joins across many tables over years, think KQL job; frequent small aggregates, summary rule; archived or one-table forensic retrieval, search job.

questions.question: Contoso wants Defender for Endpoint to remediate confirmed threats on user workstations without waiting for approval, but every remediation on the domain controllers must stay pending until an analyst reviews it. How should you configure automated investigation and response (AIR)?
options: Set the tenant-wide automation level to Full and rely on the Action Center history to undo unwanted server remediation afterward
Onboard the domain controllers to Defender for Identity instead, so AIR in Defender for Endpoint skips them
Place workstations and servers in separate device groups, with the Full automation level on the workstation group and a Semi level on the server group
Set the tenant-wide automation level to Semi and approve each workstation remediation from the Action Center as it appears
questions.explanation: The AIR automation level is a property of a device group, so two groups can behave differently: Full for workstations, Semi (approval required) for domain controllers. A tenant-wide Full level would remediate servers first and only let you undo afterward. A tenant-wide Semi level forces manual approval for the workstations too, which is what you want to avoid. Defender for Identity covers the domain controllers' identity signals but does not change how AIR treats a device that is onboarded to Defender for Endpoint.

questions.question: Two Sentinel automation rules are scoped to the same analytics rule. One pages the on-call analyst (order 2). Another closes incidents caused by a known vulnerability scanner as benign (order 3). The on-call analyst is still being paged for incidents that then get auto-closed. What should you change?
options: Delete and recreate the auto-close rule, because the most recently created automation rule runs first
Rename the auto-close rule so that it sorts alphabetically ahead of the paging rule
Move the auto-close condition into the paging rule's playbook, because playbooks run before automation rules
Give the auto-close rule a lower order number than the paging rule, so it evaluates first
questions.explanation: Automation rules run in ascending order number, and a rule's conditions are evaluated when its turn comes, so the auto-close rule must have the lower number to act before the paging rule. Names and creation dates play no part in ordering. Playbooks are invoked by automation rules, not ahead of them, so a check inside the playbook would run only after the page had already been requested.
questions.whyTested: Candidates often assume implicit ordering (by name, by creation date, or playbooks first). The exam tests the one real mechanism: the explicit order number on each automation rule.

questions.question: A Sentinel playbook must, when it runs for a case, loop through every alert and every account, host and IP entity in that case and look each one up in a reputation service. Which Logic Apps trigger should the playbook use?
options: When a response to a Microsoft Sentinel entity is triggered (entity trigger)
When a response to a Microsoft Sentinel alert is triggered (alert trigger)
When Microsoft Sentinel incident creation rule was triggered (incident trigger)
When an HTTP request is received, with the Sentinel connector added later
questions.explanation: The incident trigger hands the playbook the whole incident object, from which it can pull all correlated alerts and entities. The alert trigger exposes only one alert's data, the entity trigger runs manually against a single entity from the investigation graph, and a bare HTTP trigger carries no Sentinel context unless you build it yourself.

questions.question: Contoso must raise an incident within about a minute whenever a new member is added to a privileged Entra role. The audit events arrive in a supported table, and the detection needs only a simple query. A 5-minute scheduled rule was rejected as too slow. Which analytics rule type should you create?
options: Near-real-time (NRT) rule
Fusion rule that correlates the audit events with other alerts
Microsoft security rule that mirrors Entra ID Protection alerts
Scheduled rule with a 1-minute frequency and a 1-minute lookback
questions.explanation: NRT rules run about once a minute against a simple query on supported tables, which fits the latency need. A scheduled rule cannot be set below its 5-minute minimum frequency, so a 1-minute schedule is not an option. A Microsoft security rule only mirrors alerts another product already raised, and Fusion is an ML engine that correlates multiple weak signals rather than evaluating your own query.

questions.question: Firewall logs reach Sentinel through the CEF connector using Azure Monitor Agent. Debug-level messages make up about 60 percent of the volume, are never queried, and drive up ingestion cost. How do you cut the cost?
options: Add a transformation to the Data Collection Rule that drops the debug rows before ingestion
Reduce the table's retention period so the debug rows age out sooner
Create a summary rule that aggregates the raw rows into a smaller table
Add a where clause excluding debug rows to each analytics rule that reads the table
questions.explanation: An ingestion-time transformation in the DCR removes rows before they are stored, so they are never billed as ingestion. Filtering in analytics rules changes what a query returns but the full volume is still ingested. Retention affects how long data is kept, not what is charged at ingestion. A summary rule creates an additional table from data already ingested, so the raw volume is still paid for.

questions.question: A CISO wants a matrix view of which MITRE ATT&CK techniques currently have no enabled analytics rule or hunting query in the Sentinel workspace, to decide where detection engineering effort should go next. Which should the SOC use?
options: Threat analytics in the Microsoft Defender portal
The Analytics efficiency workbook
The regulatory compliance dashboard in Defender for Cloud
The MITRE ATT&CK page in Microsoft Sentinel
questions.explanation: The MITRE ATT&CK page maps the workspace's own rules and queries to techniques and shows where nothing covers a technique. Threat analytics reports on specific named threats and whether you are exposed to them. The Analytics efficiency workbook measures how well existing rules perform, not technique coverage. The regulatory compliance dashboard maps Azure resource configuration to named standards, not ATT&CK.

questions.question: In advanced hunting, an analyst uses Security Copilot to generate a KQL query from a plain-language description and now wants to turn it into a custom detection rule that runs on a schedule. What should the analyst do first?
options: Recreate the query by hand, because a Copilot-generated query is not accepted by custom detections
Save it directly as a rule, because Copilot validates generated queries against the schema and tenant data
Run the query and review its logic and results to confirm it finds the intended behavior
Ask Copilot to confirm the query's accuracy, then publish without running it
questions.explanation: Security Copilot accelerates drafting, but the analyst remains responsible for confirming the query does what was intended before it becomes an automated detection. Schema validity does not prove the logic is right or that false positives are acceptable. Asking Copilot to grade its own output is not independent validation. There is no restriction that stops a generated query from backing a custom detection once it has been reviewed.

questions.question: HR sends a weekly CSV of about 300 terminated employees' UPNs. Sentinel analytics rules must alert on any sign-in by these accounts, and the SOC wants to replace the list each week without editing any rule's KQL. What should you use?
options: A dynamic array defined in a let statement at the top of each rule
A Sentinel watchlist, referenced in the rules with the _GetWatchlist() function
Threat intelligence indicators imported through the threat intelligence blade
A workbook parameter populated from the CSV
questions.explanation: A watchlist is analyst-curated reference data imported from CSV and queried with _GetWatchlist(), so refreshing the list requires no change to the rules. Threat intelligence indicators describe threat artifacts such as malicious IPs, domains and hashes, with confidence and expiry, not an HR roster. A let array would have to be edited in every rule. A workbook parameter exists only inside a workbook and cannot feed an analytics rule.

questions.question: On a user's entity page, Sentinel shows that she accessed a SharePoint site for the first time and that no one else in her peer group has ever touched it. No analytics rule is configured for this activity. Which feature produced the finding?
options: The Microsoft security analytics rule type
A scheduled rule joined to a watchlist of SharePoint sites
Fusion advanced multistage attack detection
User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA)
questions.explanation: UEBA builds baselines per entity and against its peer group, then surfaces first-time or unusual activity as enrichment without any rule being authored. Fusion correlates several lower-fidelity alerts into one incident and needs alerts to exist. A scheduled rule with a watchlist would need someone to write it. The Microsoft security rule type only turns another product's existing alerts into incidents.

questions.question: A SOC installs a content hub solution for a new firewall vendor. The data connector shows data arriving and the table is populated, but a week later there are no incidents from it. Which should you check first?
options: Whether the solution's data connector DCR has a transformation that removes the alert fields
Whether analytics rules were actually created from the solution's rule templates and are enabled
Whether the lookback of the solution's workbook is long enough to show historical alerts
Whether the workspace's UEBA baseline has finished syncing for the firewall's devices
questions.explanation: Installing a solution stages its analytics rule templates; nothing generates incidents until a rule is created from a template and enabled. A DCR transformation could hide fields, but that is a less likely cause than rules never being enabled. UEBA baselines do not gate analytics rules, and a workbook only visualizes data and has no effect on incident creation.

questions.question: A scheduled rule is configured to group alerts into one incident when the Account entity matches. Two alerts minutes apart concern the same user, yet they create two separate incidents. The query output includes the user's UPN in a plain column. What should you do?
options: Extend the rule's query lookback to the maximum of 14 days
Map that column to the Account entity in the rule's entity mapping
Set event grouping to trigger a single alert for all events
Add an automation rule that merges incidents with the same owner
questions.explanation: Alert grouping compares mapped entities, so a UPN that is not mapped to an Account entity cannot be matched across alerts. Event grouping controls how many alerts a single query run produces, not whether separate alerts merge into an incident. Query lookback changes which events are scanned, not how alerts are grouped. Automation rules can change owner and severity but are not the mechanism for merging alerts by entity here.
questions.whyTested: Four Sentinel tuning settings all sound like they influence incident merging. Only entity mapping decides whether two alerts share an entity at all, which is what entity-based alert grouping relies on.

questions.question: A vulnerability scanner's IP addresses change every month and IT maintains the current list. A brute-force analytics rule keeps raising false positives from them. You want these sources excluded so no alert or incident is created, without editing the rule when the list changes. What should you do?
options: Hardcode the current scanner IPs in the rule query and update them each month
Create an automation rule that closes the resulting incidents as benign
Enable alert suppression on the rule for 24 hours
Keep the scanner IPs in a watchlist and exclude them via _GetWatchlist()
questions.explanation: Excluding a watchlist in the query stops the alerts from being generated and lets IT change the list without touching the rule. Hardcoded addresses work today but require a rule edit every month. An automation rule closes incidents that were still created, leaving alert noise and wasted triage. Suppression only pauses the rule temporarily and for all sources, not just the scanner.

questions.question: A SOC subscribes to a TAXII feed of malicious IP addresses. Each indicator has a confidence score and expires after 30 days. Detections must match sign-in IPs against these indicators and ignore expired ones. Which approach fits?
options: Import the feed as threat intelligence indicators and use the TI-based analytics rule templates
Import the feed as a watchlist and join it with _GetWatchlist() in a scheduled rule
Add the feed's IP addresses as a custom indicator in Defender for Endpoint
Ingest the feed into a custom _CL table and write a separate rule for each indicator type
questions.explanation: Threat intelligence indicators carry confidence and validity dates, land in the ThreatIntelIndicators table (which replaced the legacy ThreatIntelligenceIndicator table), and are matched by built-in TI analytics rule templates that honor expiry. A watchlist is static reference data with no concept of indicator expiry or confidence. A custom table duplicates what the TI blade already provides. A Defender for Endpoint indicator blocks or alerts on devices but does not match Entra sign-in logs in Sentinel.

questions.question: A SOC manager wants a live dashboard of incident volume and mean time to close for executives with Reader access, and also wants someone alerted whenever mean time to close exceeds four hours. Which design meets both needs?
options: A playbook for the dashboard, plus an automation rule for the threshold alert
A workbook for the dashboard, plus a scheduled analytics rule over SecurityIncident for the threshold alert
A single workbook that also generates incidents when a tile crosses the threshold
A hunting query bookmark for the dashboard, plus a saved hunting query run each morning for the threshold alert
questions.explanation: Workbooks visualize KQL results for human readers but cannot raise incidents themselves, so the alerting need requires a scheduled analytics rule querying SecurityIncident. A playbook performs actions and does not render dashboards, and an automation rule reacts to incidents rather than measuring a metric. Bookmarks preserve hunting evidence, and a saved hunting query is run by hand and raises no alert on its own.

questions.question: A sales rep's Windows laptop is compromised. The rep must stay on a customer Teams call and keep reading mail in Outlook, while the SOC cuts the device off from everything else and keeps Defender for Endpoint telemetry flowing. Which response should the analyst use?
options: Use the isolation option that still allows Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business
Apply Restrict app execution so only Microsoft-signed apps can run on the laptop
Use full isolation, which keeps just the connection to Defender for Endpoint
Apply the Contain device action, which restricts communication with the laptop
questions.explanation: Selective isolation is the isolation option that keeps Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business connectivity while blocking other traffic, and the device stays connected to the Defender for Endpoint service. Full isolation would drop the call and mail. Contain device is meant for devices that are not onboarded, and Restrict app execution limits which apps may run without cutting off the network.

questions.question: An analyst must run one of the team's prepared scripts on a flagged server, then download one specific file from it, immediately and without waiting for any automated process. Which Defender for Endpoint capability fits?
options: Run antivirus scan
Initiate automated investigation
Collect investigation package
Live response
questions.explanation: Live response opens an interactive remote shell on the device where the analyst can run uploaded scripts, fetch a chosen file and stop processes. Collecting an investigation package gathers a fixed set of forensic data into an archive but offers no commands. An antivirus scan only scans, and an automated investigation follows its own playbook rather than the analyst's commands.

questions.question: At the Full automation level, AIR quarantined a legitimate internal tool on 40 devices yesterday. The tool must be restored, and it must not be flagged again. What should the analyst do?
options: Switch the device group to a Semi level and rerun the automated investigation on the devices
Undo the quarantines from Action Center history and add an allow indicator for the hash
Delete the alert that triggered the automated investigation, which reverses its actions
Reject the quarantine actions in the Action Center's pending actions list for the device group
questions.explanation: Completed remediation shows in the Action Center history, where supported actions such as quarantine can be undone, and an allow indicator for the hash keeps the file from being flagged again. The actions are no longer pending, so there is nothing left to reject. Changing the automation level affects future investigations without restoring the file, and deleting an alert reverses nothing.

questions.question: A custom indicator set to Block for a malicious domain works in Microsoft Edge, but users on Google Chrome can still browse to it. What must be enabled so the block also applies to Chrome?
options: A Safe Links policy covering the domain
An allow indicator for the Chrome executable
Cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Network protection in block mode on the devices
questions.explanation: Domain and IP indicators are enforced through SmartScreen in Edge and through network protection for other browsers, so network protection in block mode is needed for Chrome. Cloud-delivered protection supports file indicators, Safe Links is a Defender for Office 365 control for links in messages and Office apps, and allowing the Chrome executable does nothing to restrict a destination.

questions.question: A phishing campaign was reported after many messages had already reached mailboxes. An analyst must find every recipient and the delivery location of each message by sender and subject, then soft-delete the messages from the mailboxes. Which tool fits?
options: Threat Explorer in Defender for Office 365
The Submissions page in the Defender portal
Attack simulation training in Defender for Office 365
Message trace in the Exchange admin center
questions.explanation: Threat Explorer searches delivered mail by sender, subject and delivery action, and lets the analyst start remediation such as soft delete straight from the results. Message trace shows routing but offers no remediation. Attack simulation training sends practice phishing to users, and the Submissions page lists what users or admins reported, not an investigation across mailboxes.

questions.question: A message looked clean when delivered, but updated signatures later classified it as malware. It was moved from the inbox to quarantine without any analyst approving an action. Which capability moved it?
options: Threat Explorer with a remediation action
Automated investigation and response in Defender for Office 365
Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP)
Safe Attachments Dynamic Delivery
questions.explanation: ZAP acts automatically on already-delivered mail whose verdict changes after delivery. Automated investigation in Defender for Office 365 produces recommended actions that typically wait in the Action Center for approval. Dynamic Delivery works before delivery by holding the attachment while scanning, and Threat Explorer remediation is started by an analyst.

questions.question: Defender for Identity flags a chain of computers and cached credentials an attacker could use to eventually reach a Domain Admin account, even though no attack is currently in progress. What is this finding called, and what does it represent?
options: A lateral movement path -- a proactive exposure finding showing what a compromise could reach, not an active attack
A honeytoken alert -- a high-confidence signal that a decoy account was touched, not a mapped chain of reachable credentials
A Fusion incident -- a machine-learning correlation of several lower-fidelity alerts into one higher-confidence case
A regulatory compliance failure -- a gap against a specific standard's control requirement, unrelated to credential exposure
questions.explanation: A lateral movement path is a proactive, exposure-focused finding mapping what an attacker could reach through cached credentials, distinct from an alert about an attack already happening. A honeytoken alert or Fusion incident would instead reflect actual observed malicious activity, and this has nothing to do with a compliance standard.

questions.question: Contoso creates an enabled account named svc-backup-old that no person or service should ever use. Defender for Identity must raise a high-confidence alert on any authentication attempt that involves it. How should the account be configured in Defender for Identity?
options: Tag it as a sensitive account
Add it to an exclusion so activity is not noisy
Add it to the Domain Admins group for visibility
Tag it as a honeytoken account
questions.explanation: Tagging an unused decoy account as a honeytoken makes any activity involving it an alert, since no legitimate user has a reason to touch it. A sensitive tag marks high-value accounts such as admins to extend detections and lateral movement path analysis, an exclusion suppresses detections, and adding an unused account to Domain Admins creates risk without producing detections.

questions.question: An organization wants to block a user from downloading a file from a sanctioned cloud app during an active, already-authenticated session, based on real-time conditions like an unmanaged device. Which capability enforces this?
options: A Conditional Access App Control access policy, evaluated only at sign-in before the session starts
A Sentinel automation rule triggered on incident creation
Defender for Endpoint live response targeting the user's device directly
Conditional Access App Control with a session policy
questions.explanation: Conditional Access App Control routes the session through Defender for Cloud Apps as a reverse proxy, and a session policy can then enforce real-time, in-session controls like blocking a download. An access policy only gates whether the session is allowed to start, not what happens inside it once authenticated, and a Sentinel automation rule or Defender for Endpoint live response operate on incidents and endpoints, not live in-session cloud app enforcement.
questions.whyTested: SC-200 repeatedly probes the access-policy-versus-session-policy line inside Conditional Access App Control, because it's a subtle 'before versus during the session' distinction that's easy to gloss over -- one of the four options here is worded to look like the right answer while actually just describing the access policy again.

questions.question: Contoso wants Defender for Cloud Apps to alert when any single user downloads more than 30 files from SharePoint Online within five minutes, using thresholds the SOC chooses. Which policy type should be created?
options: An anomaly detection policy
A session policy
A file policy
An activity policy
questions.explanation: Activity policies let you define the activity, the count threshold and the time window yourself. Anomaly detection policies, such as impossible travel, use built-in machine learning baselines and are tuned by sensitivity rather than explicit thresholds. A session policy acts on a live proxied session, and a file policy inspects file content and metadata at rest.

questions.question: During a ransomware campaign, Defender XDR correlated signals across several workloads and, with no custom rule configured and no analyst approval, disabled the compromised account and contained the devices being used. Which capability did this?
options: A custom detection rule with response actions
A Conditional Access sign-in risk policy
Automated investigation and response at the Full automation level
Automatic attack disruption
questions.explanation: Automatic attack disruption uses high-confidence cross-workload signals to contain users and devices at machine speed. AIR investigates alerts and remediates artifacts such as files, rather than containing accounts across an incident. A custom detection rule performs actions only if someone built it, and a sign-in risk policy governs future sign-ins rather than containing devices.

questions.question: After the Microsoft Defender XDR connector is enabled in Sentinel with incident synchronization, analysts see two incidents for each Defender for Endpoint alert: one synchronized from Defender XDR and one created by Sentinel. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: Microsoft security analytics rules also create incidents for those alerts; disable those rules
Alert grouping is set too narrow; widen the grouping time window on the rules
Fusion is correlating the alerts a second time; disable the Fusion rule
Bidirectional synchronization copies incidents instead of linking them; turn synchronization off
questions.explanation: When Defender XDR incidents are already synchronized, a Microsoft security rule that creates incidents from the same product's alerts produces duplicates, so those rules should be disabled. Synchronization links one incident across both portals and does not duplicate it, Fusion does not create incidents from every alert, and alert grouping applies only to alerts that Sentinel rules generate.

questions.question: A hunting query joins DeviceNetworkEvents (a very large table) to DeviceLogonEvents on DeviceId. Only RDP connections (RemotePort 3389) from the last day matter on the network side, and only the last day of logons. Which structure is most efficient?
options: Filter just the logon table, because the join key already limits the network rows
Join the two full tables first, then apply the time and port filters to the joined result
Filter each table by time, and the network table by port, before the join
Join first, then use summarize to discard the rows that fall outside the filters
questions.explanation: KQL runs operators in the order written, so filtering each input before the join means the join works on far fewer rows. Joining first makes the engine process the full tables, and summarize afterwards only adds work. Relying on the join key does not shrink the network table, which is the bigger side.

questions.question: A hunting query that an analyst runs manually every week keeps finding genuine C2 beaconing. The SOC wants an incident created automatically each time it matches, with the host and IP attached as entities, and no analyst needing to remember to run it. What should the analyst do?
options: Mark the hunting query as a favorite so it runs with the other favorites
Save the matching rows as a bookmark and add it to a new incident each week
Pin the query to a workbook tile so the team can see the matches
Create a scheduled analytics rule from the query and map the host and IP entities
questions.explanation: Promoting a proven hunting query into a scheduled analytics rule makes detection automatic, and entity mapping attaches the host and IP to the incident. A bookmark preserves one set of results by hand, a workbook tile only displays results without creating incidents, and favorites only make queries easier to run manually.

questions.question: A SOC analyst used a hunting query to find a suspicious pattern and now wants it to notify the team persistently whenever new matching events arrive, replacing the retired Sentinel livestream feature. Which approach is recommended?
options: A bookmark on the query's current results
A scheduled or near-real-time analytics rule, with a playbook for notification
A watchlist containing the matching events
A workbook tile that is opened daily
questions.explanation: Livestream is no longer available; analytics rules (and playbooks or KQL jobs) provide persistent detection and notification. A bookmark captures results that already exist, a watchlist is reference data rather than a notifier, and a workbook tile must be opened by someone to be seen.

questions.question: A hunting query must list the accounts in a privileged-users watchlist that have no sign-in in SigninLogs over the last 7 days. The result should hold only watchlist rows, in a single join with no extra null filtering. Which join kind fits?
options: leftanti
leftouter
leftsemi
inner
questions.explanation: leftanti returns only the left-side rows that have no match on the right, which is exactly the watchlist accounts without a sign-in. leftouter keeps every left row, so you would then have to filter out the matched ones. leftsemi returns the opposite set (left rows that do match), and inner returns matched pairs only.
questions.whyTested: Negative questions such as 'accounts with no sign-in' tempt people to pick inner or leftouter. Reasoning about which rows each join kind returns shows that leftanti is the direct answer.

questions.question: A hunting query keeps a dynamic list of suspicious executable names in a let statement. FileName values arrive in mixed case, such as PowerShell.exe and powershell.exe, and each must match a list entry exactly, ignoring case. Which filter should the query use?
options: | where FileName in~ (suspicious)
| where FileName matches regex suspicious
| where FileName has_any (suspicious)
| where FileName in (suspicious)
questions.explanation: in~ tests membership in a list and ignores case. in is case-sensitive, so PowerShell.exe would be missed if the list holds powershell.exe. has_any matches terms inside the value rather than the whole value, so it also hits names like powershell.exe.bak, and matches regex does not accept a list variable.

questions.question: In Defender XDR advanced hunting, an analyst wants every process launched under the account of anyone who received a particular phishing email. Which join condition between EmailEvents and DeviceProcessEvents links the recipient to the process?
options: $left.SenderFromDomain == $right.DeviceName
$left.SenderFromAddress == $right.AccountUpn
$left.RecipientEmailAddress == $right.AccountUpn
$left.NetworkMessageId == $right.ReportId
questions.explanation: The recipient's email address identifies the user who received the message, and AccountUpn on the process event identifies the account that launched the process. The sender is the attacker, not the victim. NetworkMessageId and ReportId are unrelated identifiers, and a sender domain does not map to a device name.

questions.question: Automatically closing a Sentinel incident that matches a known-benign pattern requires a playbook, because automation rules cannot change an incident's status on their own.
questions.explanation: Automation rules can change status, close an incident with a classification, assign an owner, change severity, add tags and add tasks without invoking any playbook. A playbook is needed only when the response calls an external system or does something an automation rule has no built-in action for.

questions.question: A near-real-time (NRT) analytics rule in Sentinel runs on a fixed interval of about one minute, rather than letting you pick a query frequency the way a scheduled rule does.
questions.explanation: NRT rules are built for low latency: they run roughly once a minute with a fixed cadence, which is why they accept only simpler queries on supported tables. A scheduled rule lets you set its own frequency and lookback, with a minimum of five minutes.

questions.question: Shortening a Log Analytics table's retention period is an effective way to lower the ingestion charge for the data the table receives.
questions.explanation: Ingestion is billed on the volume of data accepted into the workspace, and retention only controls how long stored data is kept. To lower the ingestion charge you have to ingest less, for example by filtering rows or dropping columns with a Data Collection Rule transformation, or by choosing a cheaper table plan where its limits are acceptable.

questions.question: A Sentinel analytics rule can show as enabled with no errors and still never create an incident, simply because the table its query reads has no data.
questions.explanation: A rule only evaluates the query it is given. If the connector for its source table is missing or misconfigured, the query returns nothing and the rule stays silent without reporting a failure. Checking data connector health and table contents is a standard first step when an enabled rule seems dead.

questions.question: When the contents of a Sentinel watchlist change, every analytics rule that references the watchlist must be edited and re-saved before it uses the new data.
questions.explanation: Rules reference a watchlist by its alias through _GetWatchlist(), and the function reads the watchlist's current contents each time the query runs. Updating the watchlist therefore changes rule behavior without touching any rule, which is the main reason to prefer a watchlist over values hardcoded in KQL.

questions.question: UEBA can show an entity's activity compared with its peer group on the entity page even when no analytics rule has ever fired for that entity.
questions.explanation: UEBA builds baselines from ingested data for each user and device and compares them with peers, independent of analytics rules. The enrichment appears on entity pages and in incidents, which is why it can highlight unusual behavior that no static rule was written to catch.

questions.question: With selective isolation, an analyst can exempt any business application on the device, identified by its process name, so that it keeps network access while everything else is blocked.
questions.explanation: Selective isolation is a fixed option that keeps Outlook, Microsoft Teams and Skype for Business connected. It is not a general allow list by process name, so an arbitrary business application, such as a backup agent, would still be cut off under selective isolation. Where the newer isolation exclusions feature is enabled, admins can separately exempt specific processes, IP addresses, or services, but that is a different capability from selective isolation.

questions.question: Zero-hour auto purge is available only to tenants licensed for Defender for Office 365; a tenant with Exchange Online Protection alone does not get it.
questions.explanation: ZAP is part of Exchange Online Protection as well as Defender for Office 365, and acts on malware, phishing and spam verdicts that change after delivery. The paid plans add other capabilities such as Safe Links, Safe Attachments and Threat Explorer, which are often confused with ZAP.

questions.question: Defender for Identity can report a lateral movement path to a sensitive account even when no alert has ever been raised for any account or machine on that path.
questions.explanation: A lateral movement path is an exposure finding built from where privileged accounts have signed in and what an attacker could reach from a given machine. It shows an opportunity and does not depend on any alert having fired, which is why it is used to harden an environment before an attack.

questions.question: For a Defender for Cloud Apps session policy to apply to an app, an Entra Conditional Access policy must first route the app's sessions through Conditional Access App Control.
questions.explanation: Session control works because a Conditional Access policy with the Use Conditional Access App Control session setting sends the user's session through the Defender for Cloud Apps reverse proxy. Without that routing, the session never reaches the proxy and a session policy has nothing to act on.

questions.question: Safe Links in Defender for Office 365 can check URLs in Microsoft Teams messages and Office apps, not just in email.
questions.explanation: Safe Links protection extends beyond email to links in Teams and in Office apps, checking the destination at click time. Many people assume it is an email-only feature, but click-time checking applies wherever the policy covers the link.

questions.question: An analyst's advanced hunting query ends with summarize count() by DeviceName. Saving it as a custom detection rule fails. What change makes it valid?
options: Change DeviceName to a string literal so the output type of the query is fixed
Use arg_max so the output keeps Timestamp, ReportId and DeviceId
Add a join to the AlertInfo table so that related alerts are attached to each row
Replace summarize with project-away so that fewer columns are returned by the query
questions.explanation: A custom detection needs each result row to carry Timestamp and ReportId plus a column that identifies the affected asset, such as DeviceId. A bare count by DeviceName drops those columns, so the query must preserve the event details, typically with arg_max. Removing columns, joining to alerts or hardcoding a value does not supply the required fields.

questions.question: A KQL let variable defined in one hunting query is automatically available in every other query in the same workspace.
questions.explanation: A let statement is scoped to the query that contains it. To reuse the logic across queries you save it as a function, which other queries can then call by name, or keep the data in a watchlist.

questions.question: SigninLogs and DeviceProcessEvents both record the time of each event in a column named Timestamp.
questions.explanation: Log Analytics tables such as SigninLogs use TimeGenerated, while Defender XDR advanced hunting tables such as DeviceProcessEvents use Timestamp. Using the wrong name in a cross-source query is a common reason a time filter errors or silently matches nothing.

questions.question: Which two statements about Sentinel automation rules are true? (Choose two.)
options: Adding a tag to an incident requires a playbook to be invoked by the rule
When several automation rules match an incident, they run in no defined order
A rule can trigger on incident creation and also when an incident is updated
A rule can be given an expiration date, useful for handling during maintenance
Only one automation rule can be scoped to any given analytics rule at a time
questions.explanation: Automation rules support both an incident-created and an incident-updated trigger, and an expiration date lets a rule handle a short-lived situation, such as a maintenance window, without someone remembering to remove it. Tagging is a built-in rule action that needs no playbook, several automation rules can match the same analytics rule, and they run in ascending order number.

questions.question: Which two statements about Data Collection Rules (DCRs) and Azure Monitor Agent are true? (Choose two.)
options: A DCR transformation runs after the data is stored, so the full volume is still billed
The legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent takes its collection settings from DCRs
One DCR can be associated with many machines, and a machine can have more than one DCR associated
A workspace transformation DCR can filter data from sources that have no DCR of their own, such as diagnostic settings
questions.explanation: DCR associations are many-to-many, and the workspace transformation DCR applies transformations to tables fed by sources that do not use their own DCR. The legacy MMA agent was configured on the workspace rather than by DCRs, and a DCR transformation runs at ingestion, before storage, which is how it lowers billed volume.

questions.question: Which two statements about the Basic Logs table plan, compared with the Analytics plan, are true? (Choose two.)
options: Basic ingestion is billed at the same rate as the Analytics plan
Queries against Basic data are charged based on the amount of data scanned
Basic tables support the full KQL language, including joins across any table
Data on the Basic plan cannot be used as the source of a scheduled analytics rule
questions.explanation: Basic Logs trades lower ingestion cost for restrictions: it cannot back analytics rules, it supports a limited KQL surface, and each query is billed on data scanned. Full KQL with arbitrary joins and the same ingestion rate describe the Analytics plan.

questions.question: Which two statements about Defender for Endpoint device isolation are true? (Choose two.)
options: An isolated device is released automatically the next time it restarts
Selective isolation lets the analyst choose any process by name to keep communicating
An isolated device remains reachable for live response sessions
Selective isolation additionally lets Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business connect
questions.explanation: Isolation keeps the device connected to the Defender for Endpoint service so live response and investigation continue, and selective isolation adds Outlook, Teams and Skype for Business connectivity. It is not a per-process allow list, and the device stays isolated until an analyst releases it.

questions.question: Which two statements about zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) are true? (Choose two.)
options: ZAP removals wait in the Action Center until a security operator approves them
ZAP acts on a delivered message when its verdict changes to malware or phishing after delivery
ZAP rewrites URLs in messages so each click is checked at the time of the click
ZAP is included with Exchange Online Protection, not only with Defender for Office 365
questions.explanation: ZAP is a post-delivery control included in Exchange Online Protection that reacts when a verdict changes after delivery. Rewriting URLs for click-time checks is Safe Links, and ZAP acts automatically rather than waiting for approval, unlike many automated investigation actions.

questions.question: Which two statements about automatic attack disruption in Defender XDR are true? (Choose two.)
options: It requires a Sentinel automation rule to be configured before it can act
Actions it takes appear in the Action Center, where an analyst can undo them
It acts on every alert in the tenant, whatever the confidence level
It relies on signals correlated across several Defender workloads to reach high confidence
questions.explanation: Attack disruption works from correlated high-confidence signals and records its containment actions so they can be reviewed and reversed. It is built into Defender XDR and does not depend on Sentinel, and it is deliberately limited to high-confidence attack patterns, not every alert.

questions.question: Which two statements about KQL join kinds are true? (Choose two.)
options: leftsemi returns columns from both tables for the rows that have a match
With no kind specified, join uses innerunique, which deduplicates left-side keys
With no kind specified, join behaves as a plain inner join over both tables
leftanti returns the left-side rows that have no match on the right
questions.explanation: The default flavor is innerunique, which collapses duplicate left-side keys before matching, a frequent source of unexpectedly missing rows. leftanti keeps left rows with no match. leftsemi returns only the left-side columns, and the default is not a plain inner join.

questions.question: Which two statements about hunting features in Sentinel are true? (Choose two.)
options: A bookmark preserves selected result rows so they can be added to an incident as evidence
Livestream remains the primary way to get persistent notifications from a query
A bookmark re-runs its query every five minutes and updates itself
Livestream has been retired, so analytics rules, KQL jobs, or playbooks should be used for persistent notification
questions.explanation: Bookmarks capture evidence from a hunt and can be attached to incidents, and livestream is no longer available, with analytics rules, KQL jobs, and playbooks as the persistent alternatives. A bookmark is a stored snapshot rather than a recurring query, so it does not re-run.

questions.question:
A scheduled analytics rule contains the following KQL:

let riskyIPs = ThreatIntelIndicators
| where Confidence > 70
| project NetworkIP = ObservableValue;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| join kind=inner riskyIPs on $left.IPAddress == $right.NetworkIP
| project UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, TimeGenerated

What does this query return?
options: Every sign-in from the last day, annotated with a null NetworkIP column when no threat intelligence match exists
Only sign-ins from the last day whose IP address matches a high-confidence threat intelligence indicator
Every threat intelligence indicator regardless of whether any sign-in matched it
A syntax error, since join requires the left and right column names to be identical
questions.explanation: kind=inner keeps only rows with a matching key on both sides, so this query returns sign-ins from the last day whose IPAddress matches a high-confidence (Confidence > 70) threat intelligence indicator value. Returning every sign-in with nulls for non-matches describes a leftouter join instead, returning every indicator regardless of a sign-in match describes a rightouter join, and join explicitly supports differently named join columns through the $left. and $right. prefixes in the on clause, so this is not a syntax error.

questions.question: A firewall produces very high-volume debug logs that are queried only occasionally by an analyst running simple single-table searches during investigations. No detection will ever read them. The team wants the lowest practical ingestion cost. Which table plan fits?
options: Analytics, with the logs summarized by a summary rule
Basic Logs
Analytics, with a short retention period
Analytics, with the table's data exported to long-term archive
questions.explanation: Basic Logs offers cheaper ingestion for high-volume data that is searched occasionally and never needed by analytics rules. Analytics keeps full ingestion cost whatever the retention, a summary rule adds a table without avoiding ingestion of the raw rows, and archive is a retention state for older data rather than a cheaper way to ingest it.

questions.question: A tier 1 analyst must assign, comment on, change the status of and close Sentinel incidents, but must not create or edit analytics rules or other workspace content. Which built-in role gives the least privilege that meets this?
options: Microsoft Sentinel Reader
Microsoft Sentinel Contributor
Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator
Microsoft Sentinel Responder
questions.explanation: Responder can manage incidents, such as assigning, commenting and closing, without being able to author analytics rules. Contributor adds rule and workbook authoring, which is more than needed. Reader can only view, and Playbook Operator exists for running playbooks and does not provide incident management.

questions.question: A query in Defender XDR advanced hunting reliably finds a malicious process pattern on endpoints. The SOC wants it to run on a schedule and automatically isolate any device that matches, using only features inside the Defender portal and no playbook. What should the analyst do?
options: Create a Defender for Cloud Apps activity policy that targets the same pattern
Create a custom detection rule from the query with the isolate device response action
Create a Sentinel scheduled analytics rule and attach a playbook that isolates the device
Save the query as a bookmark so matches can be reviewed later
questions.explanation: A custom detection rule runs a hunting query on a schedule, raises alerts, and can take response actions such as isolating a device, all within Defender XDR. A Sentinel rule would need a playbook for the isolation, which the scenario excludes. A bookmark only preserves results, and activity policies watch cloud app activity rather than endpoint processes.

questions.question: Users complain that email delivery is delayed while attachments are scanned for malware, but security still wants every attachment scanned before a recipient can open it. Which Safe Attachments setting addresses both concerns?
options: Block delivery until scanning completes, holding the entire message including the body until the attachment clears
Dynamic Delivery, which delivers the message body immediately and makes the attachment available once scanning finishes
Monitor-only mode, which logs suspicious attachments for later review without blocking or delaying delivery
Disabling Safe Attachments and relying on zero-hour auto purge to catch anything malicious after the fact
questions.explanation: Dynamic Delivery delivers the email body to the recipient right away while the attachment continues scanning in the background, then makes the attachment available once scanning completes -- addressing the delay complaint while still ensuring every attachment is scanned before it can be opened. Blocking delivery until scanning completes is exactly the delay users are complaining about, monitor-only mode does not scan-and-hold at all, and disabling Safe Attachments in favor of ZAP would remove pre-open scanning entirely, relying only on a post-delivery reclassification.

questions.question: Contoso wants to be alerted, and have the app disabled automatically, whenever an OAuth app that holds Mail.Read suddenly makes an unusually high number of Microsoft Graph calls. Which capability fits?
options: An app governance policy
A Defender for Cloud Apps session policy
An Entra ID Protection risky user policy
An Entra admin consent workflow
questions.explanation: App governance policies watch the behavior of OAuth apps, such as a spike in Graph calls against granted permissions, and can alert on it or disable the app. Risky user policies respond to user risk, a session policy controls a live user session, and a consent workflow decides whether to approve new consent requests before access is granted.

questions.question:
A hunting query runs:

SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| summarize DistinctIPs = dcount(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

What does this return?
options: For each user, the count of distinct IP addresses used within each 1-hour window over the last day
The total number of sign-ins for each user over the last day, with no time bucketing
A single running total of all distinct IP addresses across every user combined
Every individual sign-in row, unaggregated, sorted by IP address
questions.explanation: summarize with dcount(IPAddress) computes the count of distinct IP addresses, grouped by UserPrincipalName and by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), which buckets rows into 1-hour windows -- so the result is, per user and per hour, how many distinct IP addresses signed in. dcount specifically counts unique values rather than every sign-in (that would be count()), the grouping is per user and per hour rather than one combined running total, and summarize aggregates rows rather than returning them unaggregated.

questions.question: Tasks on a Sentinel incident can only be added manually by an analyst after the incident exists; an automation rule has no way to add them.
questions.explanation: An automation rule can add a task list to an incident when it is created or updated, so every analyst gets the same checklist for a given incident type. Analysts can also add tasks manually, but automation is the usual way to standardize triage.

questions.question: Safe Attachments Dynamic Delivery delivers the message with its original attachment attached, relying on zero-hour auto purge to remove the attachment if scanning finds malware.
questions.explanation: Dynamic Delivery delivers the message body immediately with a placeholder where the attachment will go, and attaches the real file only after scanning finds it safe. The original attachment is never opened by the recipient before the scan completes, so it does not depend on ZAP to clean up afterward.

questions.question: In KQL, summarize by ColumnA, ColumnB with no aggregation function returns one row for each distinct combination of the two columns, the same result as distinct ColumnA, ColumnB.
questions.explanation: With no aggregation, summarize simply groups, so each unique combination yields one row, which is what distinct returns. distinct is the idiomatic spelling, but the two produce the same set of rows.

questions.question: Which two statements about built-in Microsoft Sentinel roles are true? (Choose two.)
options: Reader can close the incidents it is able to view in the workspace
Playbook Operator can edit analytics rules and automation rules
Responder can change an incident's status and assign it, but cannot edit analytics rules
Contributor can create and edit analytics rules and workbooks in the workspace
Contributor includes permission to author the Logic Apps that back playbooks
questions.explanation: Responder manages incidents without authoring content, while Contributor adds authoring of analytics rules and workbooks. Reader is view-only. Building the Logic Apps behind playbooks needs Logic App permissions on the playbook's resource group, which Sentinel Contributor does not supply, and Playbook Operator is limited to running playbooks.

questions.question: Which two statements about KQL row-limiting operators are true? (Choose two.)
options: top works only on numeric columns and rejects datetime columns in the sort
top 10 by Timestamp desc returns the rows with the latest Timestamp
take returns an arbitrary set of rows, with no guarantee about which ones
take 10 returns the ten most recent rows by default, ordered by time
questions.explanation: take is for quick sampling and gives no ordering guarantee, while top sorts by the chosen column and then returns the first N rows. take has no notion of recency, and top works on any sortable column, including datetime.

questions.question: An external auditor must read only the AuditLogs table in the Sentinel workspace and nothing else, including other tables and incidents. How should access be granted?
options: A custom role scoped to the workspace with read on only the AuditLogs table
Assign the Log Analytics Reader role on the resource group that contains the workspace
Assign the Microsoft Sentinel Reader role on the workspace to the auditor's account
Assign the Microsoft Entra Security Reader role to the auditor's account in the tenant
questions.explanation: Table-level RBAC lets a custom role grant read access to a named table in a workspace. Sentinel Reader and Log Analytics Reader both expose data across the workspace rather than a single table. The Entra Security Reader role covers Entra security information and does not scope access to one Log Analytics table.

questions.question: A Data Collection Rule must drop incoming rows whose Severity column equals 'Debug' before they are stored. Which transformKql in the DCR achieves this?
options: source | where Severity != 'Debug'
source | summarize count() by Severity
source | project-away Severity
AppAudit_CL | where Severity != 'Debug'
questions.explanation: A DCR transformation reads the incoming stream as source, and a where clause removes the unwanted rows before storage. Referencing the destination table name is not how a transformation addresses its input. project-away removes a column but keeps every row, and summarize collapses the data into counts and loses the detail you meant to keep.

questions.question: An automation rule with the 'When incident is created' trigger sets the owner and severity of new incidents. Later, an analyst raises an incident's severity to High, and the SOC wants a playbook to notify management at that moment. What should you do?
options: Change the analytics rule's alert grouping so a severity change creates a new incident
Create another automation rule with the 'When incident is updated' trigger and a condition on the severity change
Attach an alert-trigger playbook to the analytics rule, which fires when incident severity changes
Add the notify action to the existing creation rule, which re-evaluates whenever an incident changes
questions.explanation: A rule on the incident-created trigger evaluates only when the incident is created, so a later severity change needs a rule on the incident-updated trigger with a condition on that change. The creation rule does not re-run on updates. An alert-trigger playbook reacts to alerts, not to analyst edits of an incident, and alert grouping controls how alerts merge, not what happens on a severity change.

questions.question: A compliance auditor needs to browse Sentinel incidents, workbooks and logs and run queries, but must not be able to change an incident's status or assign it. Which built-in role gives the least privilege that works?
options: Microsoft Sentinel Contributor
Microsoft Sentinel Responder
Microsoft Entra Security Administrator
Microsoft Sentinel Reader
questions.explanation: Sentinel Reader allows viewing incidents, workbooks and data without modifying incidents. Responder can change status and assign owners, Contributor adds content authoring, and an Entra Security Administrator role grants far broader rights in Entra security settings than the auditor needs.

questions.question: An analyst suspects business email compromise. Which two findings, taken together, most strongly point to a compromised account rather than normal user behavior? (Choose two.)
options: A rule forwarding mail containing 'invoice' to an external domain and marking originals as read
The mailbox size grew by a few percent over the past month, in line with earlier months
A successful MFA sign-in from an unfamiliar country, then a new inbox rule created in that session
A rule moving newsletters into a folder, created from the user's managed corporate laptop
questions.explanation: A sign-in from an unusual location that is quickly followed by a rule created in that session, together with a rule that silently forwards financial mail outside the company and hides the originals, form the classic BEC pattern. Gradual mailbox growth and a newsletter rule from a managed device are ordinary behavior.

questions.question: A query over DeviceLogonEvents in advanced hunting must return, for each device, the entire most recent logon row, including the account and logon type, not just the time. Which clause fits?
options: | distinct DeviceName, AccountName, Timestamp
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceName
| top 1 by Timestamp desc | project DeviceName, AccountName
| summarize max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName
questions.explanation: arg_max(Timestamp, *) keeps the whole row that holds the latest Timestamp in each device group. max returns only the time (plus the grouping columns) and not the rest of the row, top 1 returns a single row for the whole table rather than one per device, and distinct lists unique combinations without choosing the latest per device.

questions.question: For a Sentinel automation rule to run a playbook, Sentinel itself must be granted permissions on the resource group that contains the playbook.
questions.explanation: Automation rules run playbooks under Sentinel's own service identity, so that identity needs explicit permission (the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role) on the playbook's resource group. Without it the playbook does not appear as a selectable action or fails to run, even if the analyst creating the rule has ample rights.

questions.question: summarize max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName returns the full most recent row for each device, including every other column from that row.
questions.explanation: max returns only the maximum value, so the output has just DeviceName and the max column. To keep the entire row that has the latest time, use arg_max(TimeGenerated, *).

questions.question: In a Sentinel workspace with the Microsoft 365 and Entra ID connectors enabled, which two statements about hunting for malicious inbox rules are true? (Choose two.)
options: OfficeActivity records Exchange audit operations such as New-InboxRule
AuditLogs records Exchange mailbox rule changes made by users and admins
EmailEvents is the table where mailbox inbox rule creation is recorded
SigninLogs can be correlated with OfficeActivity on the user's UPN
questions.explanation: OfficeActivity carries Exchange audit operations including inbox rule creation, and joining it to SigninLogs on the user's identity ties a rule to the sign-in that created it. EmailEvents describes message delivery, and AuditLogs holds Entra directory changes, not mailbox rules.

questions.question: A Sentinel workspace should open an incident for every Defender for Endpoint alert of Medium severity or higher, with no KQL written for the detection itself. Which analytics rule type fits?
options: A near-real-time (NRT) rule over the SecurityAlert table
A scheduled rule that queries SecurityAlert on a timer
Fusion, with Defender for Endpoint as its data source
The Microsoft security rule type, filtered by product and severity
questions.explanation: The Microsoft security rule type turns alerts raised by a connected Microsoft product into incidents and lets you filter by product, severity and alert name, with no custom detection query. A scheduled or NRT rule would need a KQL query of its own, and Fusion correlates multiple weaker signals into one multistage incident rather than mirroring every alert.
questions.whyTested: Querying SecurityAlert on a timer is a plausible way to turn existing alerts into incidents, so it is offered as a distractor. The exam checks that you know a dedicated rule type exists for that purpose.

questions.question: A team wants every change to a Sentinel analytics rule reviewed in a pull request and then deployed to the workspace automatically, instead of being edited directly in the portal. Which Sentinel feature supports this?
options: Exporting each rule as an ARM template and deploying it by hand
Content hub, installing the team's rules as a solution
Automation rules that copy approved rules between workspaces
Repositories, connected to a GitHub or Azure DevOps repository
questions.explanation: Repositories connects a workspace to a source-control repository so merged content deploys through a pipeline, which provides review and automation together. Content hub installs vendor-packaged solutions rather than a team's own version-controlled content, a manual ARM export has no review gate or automatic deployment, and automation rules act on incidents, not on rule definitions.

questions.question: Contoso wants audit logs from an Azure SQL Database (a PaaS resource) and from a SQL Server installed on an Azure VM to reach the Sentinel workspace. How should each source be connected?
options: Diagnostic setting on the database and also on the VM
Diagnostic setting on the VM; Azure Monitor Agent with a DCR on the database
Azure Monitor Agent with a DCR on the database and also on the VM
Diagnostic setting on the Azure SQL Database; Azure Monitor Agent and DCR on the VM
questions.explanation: A PaaS resource has no operating system for an agent, so its platform logs are exported with a diagnostic setting. A SQL Server on a VM produces events inside the guest operating system, which Azure Monitor Agent collects according to a DCR. The other combinations apply each method to the wrong kind of source.

questions.question: On one VM, Defender for Cloud lists a recommendation, 'Management ports should be closed', and also a security alert, 'Suspicious RDP brute force attempt'. How should the SOC treat these two findings?
options: Treat both as proof of compromise and isolate the VM immediately
Treat the recommendation as the incident, with the alert as supporting context
Investigate the alert as observed activity, and fix the recommendation as an exposure gap
Close the port and dismiss the alert, since closing the port resolves the attack
questions.explanation: An alert records suspicious activity that Defender for Cloud actually observed and needs investigation to learn whether the attempt succeeded. A recommendation is a standing configuration gap that reduces exposure when fixed. Closing the port prevents future attempts but does not tell you whether an earlier attempt succeeded, and a recommendation is not evidence of compromise.

questions.question: Installing Azure Monitor Agent on a Windows server is enough to start sending its Security events to the Sentinel workspace; no Data Collection Rule is required.
